title: Data Types
summary: Introduces data types: string, number and boolean. Shows how quotes mark a string, how the console evaluates arithmetic, and how typeof reports a value's type.

concepts.heading: Why types exist
points: Code is itself written as text, so the computer needs a way to tell code apart from plain text data. Quotation marks do this: everything inside them is a string, not instructions.
A data type classifies a value so the program knows how it may be used. Strings, numbers and booleans appear in virtually all languages.
String = a sequence of characters (text that is not meant to be run as code).

concepts.heading: The three basic types
points: Number: written bare, with no quotes (23, 3.14). Digits do not clash with code keywords, so no marker is needed.
Boolean: true or false, written bare in lowercase, no quotes.
(Extra) Putting quotes around a number, like "23", makes it a string, which changes how + and other operators behave.
(Extra) Other types exist (undefined, null, object, bigint, symbol); the playground lesson covers some.

concepts.heading: Trying it in the console
points: Type 2 + 3 and press Enter: the console evaluates it and prints 5.
alert(2 + 3); shows a pop-up containing 5, because the expression is evaluated before alert receives it.

typeof reports a value's type as a string: typeof 23 gives "number", typeof "a name" gives "string", typeof true gives "boolean". It is shown with parentheses in the lecture, typeof(23), but works as an operator without them.
